source_reviews.independent_solution: Take alpha: z=0 and reflection R(x,y,z)=(x,y,-z). A point is fixed iff z=0. A setwise fixed line is either wholly in alpha or perpendicular to alpha. For a transverse line, its crossing point is fixed and its direction v must have Rv parallel to v; eigenvalue +1 gives a direction parallel to alpha (then containment is necessary), eigenvalue -1 gives a normal direction. Distinguish setwise invariance of a perpendicular line from pointwise fixation.

Full line classification: a line in alpha or perpendicular to alpha coincides with its image; a line parallel to alpha but outside it has a distinct parallel image; a transverse oblique line meets its distinct image at its unique point on alpha. There is no skew case. Full plane classification: alpha itself and every plane perpendicular to alpha coincide with their images; a plane parallel to alpha but distinct from it has a distinct parallel image; a plane neither parallel nor perpendicular to alpha meets its distinct image along its trace on alpha. For beta: ax+by+cz=d, the image is ax+by-cz=d, which proves the classification, including c=0 and a=b=0 special cases.

Assume a nondegenerate segment, line and ray. Segment: every plane containing its supporting line, and its unique perpendicular-bisector plane. Indeed reflection permutes the two endpoints, fixing both or exchanging them. Line: every containing plane, and every plane perpendicular to it, at any crossing point. Ray: only planes containing its supporting line. Its unique endpoint must be fixed; a perpendicular reflection through that endpoint reverses the half-line, not the same ray.

Yes, under an explicit idealization. Approximate bilateral symmetry in an organism's body gives a natural spatial model; a manufactured ideal solid sphere has every plane through its center as a symmetry plane, and a right circular cylindrical vessel has every axial plane and its central transverse plane. Real manufactured/natural objects can depart from exact symmetry, so state the model assumption rather than claim perfect physical equality.

Let F be the figure, O its unique center, and R reflection in a symmetry plane alpha. R(F)=F. For central inversion C_O, conjugation gives R C_O R^{-1}=C_{R(O)} (directly R(2O-X)=2R(O)-R(X)). Hence R(O) is also a symmetry center of F. Uniqueness of O forces R(O)=O; the fixed locus of R is alpha, so O lies in alpha. This does not need uniqueness of the symmetry plane, even if that stronger premise is read into the prose.

Yes. Construct A=(0,0,0), B=(0,0,4), C=(1,2,1), D=(-1,2,1). The four points are noncoplanar (determinant of AB, AC, AD is 16). Reflection x=0 fixes A,B and exchanges C,D, so is a symmetry. Edge lengths are AB=4, CD=2, AC=AD=sqrt(6), BC=BD=sqrt(14); all four length classes are distinct. Incident-edge signatures uniquely distinguish A and B and give C,D the only shared signature. An isometry preserving the tetrahedron must therefore fix A,B and either fix or exchange C,D. A plane reflection cannot fix all four noncoplanar vertices; exchanging C,D requires exactly their perpendicular-bisector plane x=0. Thus this tetrahedron has exactly one symmetry plane.
